Keenum found himself back in the starter’s role following the Week 2 injury to Caleb Williams during the Bears’ 9-3 loss to the Vikings. He suffered a hamstring injury during the fourth quarter of the game.

articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the weekend incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor"
Speaking to US media, he doesn't give further details but thanks UK authorities for being "co-operative" and "helpful"
Five men arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base, which is used by the US military, were released on bail on Monday - here's what else we know
The men - all UK nationals in their 20s who live in London - had been arrested under the Explosives Act and on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act
AC Laurence Taylor, the head of UK counter terrorism policing, has said officers are pursuing multiple lines of inquiry, including if proxies working on behalf of a foreign state could've been involved - the Iranian embassy in the UK denies involvement
A large cordon remains in place near the base, with 85 households being told they can return home after an evacuation on Sunday
One local tells the BBC those who've gone home are being told to stay inside and not to take photos. "I want to wait until I know more... it feels super dodge to me," she says
Edited by Steve Mellen, with Marie Lennon reporting from the scene
Security remains high at RAF Fairford, with armed police at checkpoints talking to drivers and checking cars on approach roads.

Marie Lennon Reporting from the scene
In the village of Fairford, people are trying their best to return to normal life following a surreal 48 hours -  consisting of a major evacuation, the deployment of armed police, a 400m cordon and a bomb disposal robot.
Butcher Andrew Butler describes an air of uncertainty and paranoia among residents, as they discuss the latest developments in his shop.
"A
lot of people are anxious about whatâs been going on," he says.
"But then a lot of
people are saying âwell, you know, this is a consequence of living near an
airbase', particularly one that is currently bombing another country."
Butler recalls an incident on Monday where a van, which had been parked "for quite a while", was suddenly swarmed by police and vehicles with flashing lights.
âObviously somebody must have reported that van being there. Thatâs the situation now - people are worried, a bit panicky.
"Any suspicious vehicle that people aren't sure about, they think could potentially be a problem."
Despite all the closures outside RAF Fairford, there is still activity inside.
This B1-b Lancer bomber was photographed taking off from the base this morning.
Inside the base, patrols are operating around the perimeter.
Fairford has played a key role in the ongoing conflict involving the USA, Israel and Iran.
Lakenheath is another British air base used by US forces
Fairford is not the only UK air base used by the United States Air Force.
Over in Suffolk in the East of England are Mildenhall and Lakenheath, where the state of alert has been increased by the US to "Charlie" - the second-highest alert level.
Charlie alert is usually an indication an incident has happened or intelligence suggests there could be a potential attack.
Lakenheath is home to fighter jets, while Mildenhall is mainly used as a base for refuelling tankers.
In his speech at the Labour Party conference on Monday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he couldn't provide much further detail about the terror probe at RAF Fairford beyond what has already been reported.
Instead he praised the strength of the UK-US alliance.
"Our friendship with America is the closest alliance of any two nations on Earth, and we will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm," he said.
"What we saw yesterday from our security services, our armed forces and our police was just a small glimpse of the extraordinary work they do every day."
Over the past few days a large number of emergency personnel have been basing themselves at Fairford Town Football Club.
The scene there this morning is "very quiet", our photographer says.
Bea Swallow Live page reporter
RAF Fairford is a military airfield located in the Gloucestershire Cotswolds, about four miles (6.4km) south of the town of Fairford.
It is owned by the UK's Ministry of Defence (MoD), but is operated on a day-to-day basis by the United States Air Force (USAF) under an agreement between the UK and US.
The site shares a long history with the American military, and has recently been used by US warplanes as a staging post for strikes on Iran due to its long runway, from which it can quickly deploy large bombers.
Historically, aircraft launched from the site have been involved in the Gulf War, the Kosovo War, and the Iraq War.
The rural area is typically quiet but about 170,000 people descend on the site every July for the Royal International Air Tattoo, the largest military show in the world.
The event was cancelled this year due to the war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Matty Edwards Live page reporter
Here's some more from Whelford councillor Tristan Wilkinson, who has been speaking to BBC Radio Gloucestershire.
He is calling for RAF Fairford to communicate better and make it as easy as possible to report any concerns.
"The one thing I will be pressing the authorities for in the coming days is that we have a clear way of raising concerns, so that - god forbid if somebody sees some suspicious activity in the coming weeks - everyone knows the right number to call and that number will be answered quickly," he says.
"We need to make sure the communities living next to these potential threats are well informed and involved in some of the decision making," he adds.
"I can understand why there isn't an ongoing dialogue with the base about their operational activity, but I do think there are things we could put in place that inform and reassure the local community about what is going on."
Wilkinson is also urging the wider community to show "tolerance" and "understanding" towards the evacuated residents as they deal with the disruption.
Matty Edwards Live page reporter
It will take "a considerable amount of time" for life in the village of Whelford to return to normal, according to the local councillor for the area.
Councillor Tristan Wilkinson tells BBC Radio Gloucestershire that the mood among residents is a mixture of "confusion" and "weariness".
The vast majority of residents have now gone home, he says, but some who live near to the cordon around the white vans are subject to tighter restrictions.
"I don't think there's going to be anything normal about Whelford for quite a considerable amount of time," he says.
"Even when the police leave and they deem the area to be completely safe, as long as the conflict in the Middle East carries on, the people of Whelford and Kempsford are going to be living next to an operational base, so I think it's really important that the message of vigilance stays top of people's minds," he says.
"I think the mood is predominantly one of confusion, because obviously there are different stories emerging about what the nature of this was," he adds.
"People are really keen to understand what actually happened, who were these people and what was their intention."
He says after disruption and the small village becoming an international news story over the last two days "people just want to get on with their lives".
The cordon around the three vans has been in place since Sunday.
But some residents are beginning to enter and leave the cordon this morning on the western side.

All five are UK nationals, it said: a 24-year-old from Camden, north London, three men aged 23, 24 and 25 from Westminster, and one aged 24 from Willes

In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds “wasteful” and “harmful.”
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse.
A “pocket rescission” is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a “ pocket veto ,” a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress’s adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the “pocket rescission” aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention.
The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA).
The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon’s heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president’s ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President’s rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned.
Trump’s request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect.
It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated.
The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would “cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.”
“If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law,” it continues.
Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an “abuse” of the ICA.
“It’s perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds,” Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of “historical practice.”
The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond.
In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated.
The government “shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates,” he says.
He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President.
Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: “The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, ‘Well, we're just not going to do those.’”
The Supreme Court’s intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges.
The largest portion of this year’s proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump’s request would withdraw $567 million from those services.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.
The Housing and Urban Development Department’s housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with “divisive and DEI-centric agendas.”
The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs.
“I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with,” Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to “establish stronger executive control over spending.”
The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached.
“If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?” he asks.
The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would “work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

articles.title_orig: Senate passes bipartisan bill to overhaul college sports
articles.title_zh: Senate passes bipartisan bill to overhaul college sports
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Senate on Thursday approved a sweeping college sports bill to establish a federal framework for college athletics aimed at protecting student athletes — despite some pushback from Democrats who argue that it could do the opposite.
In a 77 to 22 vote, the Senate passed the bill, known as the Protect College Sports Act, with some amendments. The bill regulates college athletics, including transfer eligibility and name, image and likeness rights. Its backers argue that it will stabilize college athletics as a flood of money enters the space.
Proponents of the bill tout its uniform eligibility rules, transparency around athletic compensation and moves aimed at safeguarding opportunities in women's and Olympic sports.
Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, the bill's sponsor, said it is aimed at quelling the "uncontrollable bidding wars" that could lead colleges to drop less lucrative college sports.
"The system we have today is unsustainable, plain and simple. Students are transferring three and four times, pros are trying to play ball against college kids, conflicting court decisions have created a fragmented system, one that no one intended. And young men and women are losing opportunities to compete and receive an education," GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, the bill's sponsor, said. "The question before this body is whether we will act or stand by while the institution that Americans have known and loved for generations — college sports — is fundamentally changed."
The bill would adopt a revenue-sharing framework outlined in a settlement agreement , which allows universities to share roughly $21.6 million with athletes for the 2026-2027 school year, along with an athlete retention fund with an additional $22.5 million per institution.
It would also grant athletes one transfer without losing eligibility, and impose health and safety protections for athletes, among other things.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune praised the bill in recent days as the result of years of work, with input from coaches, athletic directors and student athletes. And the bill's passage and strong bipartisan reception came after the Big Ten and SEC athletic conferences backed the legislation, which also has the backing of the White House.
But some lawmakers and advocacy groups have voiced their opposition, like the Congressional Black Caucus, which said the bill "has failed to meaningfully incorporate the perspectives of Black athletes, Black coaches, Black agents, HBCUs, or the Congressional Black Caucus."
Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, a former college football player, took aim at the measure earlier this month on the Senate floor, sparring with the bill's main Democratic backer, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington. Booker said while there are "good things in this bill worthy of trumpeting," some major athlete groups haven't backed the bill, arguing that they know the bill "undermines their rights, undermines their collective bargaining, undermines their health and safety, creates an unequal playing field for them relative to the other monied interests in this bill, including the coaches."
"For years and years and years, I watched my own image on Madden's video game — my own image — and never got paid for that," Booker said. "And now athletes bring it to the courts and win time and time again."
Booker lamented that on name, image and likeness rights, Congress didn't take action for decades, "but as soon as athletes start winning in court their NIL rights, suddenly Congress swoops in and is saying that we're saving their NIL rights?"
"That is a lie. The reality is, they don't need Congress' beneficent actions to give them NIL rights, they've earned them in the courts," Booker argued. "What this bill actually does is it takes away rights for them to legally challenge anything that the cartel of the NCAA does. That's why the AAJ, the trial lawyers, are against this, because it undermines their ability to win more court cases in the future."
Cantwell pushed back on Booker's assertions, arguing that revenue-sharing rights in the bill could be meaningful because the settlement agreement that last year cleared the way for schools to begin paying their athletes millions of dollars could expire.
"Us recognizing that money and recognizing the revenue sharing rights is a historic first," Cantwell said.
Cantwell called the legislation the result of "a bipartisan effort to try to bring some reason to the craziness that has basically been plaguing the most important aspects of college sports." And she praised the bill for giving athletes five years of eligibility, along with its work to preserve women's and Olympic roster slots, its effort to address "skyrocketing coaches' salaries," and whistleblower and healthcare protections. She noted that the bill creates a commission made up of athletes to discuss how to move forward on issues like collective bargaining.
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut has also spoken out about the legislation, warning that it protects an exploitative system — and questioning why the Senate's focus is on college sports at this moment.
The attention on the college sports legislation comes as the Senate is preparing to leave town in the coming days until after the midterm elections.
Some senators have voiced frustration that the chamber is focusing on college sports, rather than on the affordability issues that are expected to motivate voters in November. But Senate GOP leaders had promised the bill's sponsors a vote on the legislation after the chamber returned from its August recess. And a push to address cost-of-living issues may come later this week.
CBS News' parent company, Paramount Skydance, has reported paying for lobbying for the college sports legislation in financial documents.

By 8 p.m. on Aug. 26, the great banyan tree at the center of Boshi Village is already surrounded by offerings. Bowls filled with fresh fruit, roasted meat, and other snacks are stacked rows deep among the tree’s gnarled roots. The air hangs thick with candle and incense smoke.
Locals have laid out the smorgasbord of treats as part of the Shigu festival, a series of rituals predominantly held in southern China each year that is often likened to Mexico’s Day of the Dead.
While it’s far from well-known overseas, Shigu has long been one of China’s most important and vibrant festivals. Like the Day of the Dead, it’s a centuries-old tradition to honor the deceased and draws on a rich mix of religious and folk practices.
But Shigu is also a distinctly local celebration that embodies many unique aspects of Chinese culture — and especially the culture of Chaoshan, the southern coastal region where Boshi Village is located.
Shigu — which literally translates as “feeding the lonely ghosts” — sees communities come together to care for the spirits of the departed: making offerings, chanting Buddhist scripture, and even communicating with the deceased.
It’s unclear when the festival first emerged, but references date back to at least the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279). For a long time, the Shigu festivities in Chaoshan drew bigger crowds than any other event apart from Chinese New Year.
To grasp Shigu’s significance, it’s necessary to understand how it fits into China’s traditional cosmology. According to Confucian and Taoist practices, families have a responsibility to care for the spirits of their departed loved ones, leaving offerings of food, paper money, and even alcohol to ensure they are comfortable in the afterlife.
But many people die with no children to care for their souls, while seafarers and soldiers often perish far from home and their bodies are never returned to their hometowns. If neglected, these spirits become “lonely ghosts” that wander the Earth, spreading woe and harassing the living.
The Shigu festival is designed to prevent this. Taking place in the seventh lunar month of the traditional Chinese calendar — when Yanwang, the king of hell, is said to open the gates of the underworld — communities lay out offerings for these lonely souls, giving the hungry ghosts temporary relief.
In this, Shigu differs from the Day of the Dead, which is more about families honoring their ancestors. China’s Qingming Festival in early April is perhaps a closer equivalent in that sense, though its traditions of tomb-sweeping and quiet family ceremonies are quite different.
Over the centuries, the Shigu festival has become more elaborate. Offerings are now often accompanied by communal rituals that blend Buddhist and local folk traditions. (In many places, the festival is also called “Pudu,” a name that derives from the Buddhist concept of “universal salvation” — or delivering all souls from suffering.)
In Chaoshan, many groups organize “spirit-writing” ceremonies — a practice akin to using a Ouija board to communicate with ghosts, except characters are written in sand. Others organize processions between local temples and offering grounds, led by officials chanting Buddhist scripture.
Local charities, meanwhile, donate everything from medicine to coffins to people in need in mass “merit-making ceremonies.” Most famously, the impoverished are allowed to grab the food laid out for the spirits during a ritual known as the “scramble for the offerings” — though these days the contests tend to be infiltrated by a fair number of tourists.
Today, Shigu is still marked across the Chinese-speaking world, but the celebrations are particularly central to life in Chaoshan — a reflection of the region’s turbulent history.
Chaoshan has long had a large population of hungry ghosts. For centuries, wars and uprisings across the region left countless people without a proper burial. More recently, millions set sail from Chaoshan to seek work overseas, forming large diasporas across Southeast Asia and even further afield.
To care for all these wandering souls, towns and villages across Chaoshan still mark Shigu at the end of every summer. Though the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, known as the Zhongyuan Festival, is widely regarded as the height of the Shigu festival, communities hold their ceremonies on different days throughout the month. No one is sure how and when the dates were selected.
In Nansha, a village near the city of Shantou, the Zhongyuan Festival celebrations are in full swing when Sixth Tone visits in late August. Shopkeepers unable to join the collective village ceremony set up tables outside their businesses to lay out offerings. Other villagers gather at the local temple and ancestral hall to organize the main events.
Elderly residents take charge. Some use loudspeakers to blare out appeals in Chaoshan dialect, calling on villagers to donate money and rice for the Pudu. Others fold triangular paper offerings or prepare baskets of “ guye fish rice,” a staple offering used in local rituals.
Inside the temple, a group of women performs a ceremony to honor the wandering spirits — known affectionately as guye , or lonely elders. Donated flour, rice, cooking oil, and fruit are piled in front of the temple for needy villagers to collect.
At the ancestral hall, neat stacks of rice cakes, bread, snacks, and baskets of “ guye fish rice” are arranged in a courtyard in front of the main entrance. Lin Qiwei, a local village elder, begins a ceremony to make the offerings at 3 p.m., kneeling and chanting a sacrificial text.
“Orphaned souls with no one to claim you, come here and eat,” Lin calls. “Once you have eaten your fill, return each to your place; do not disturb the living; do not frighten the children.”
After the ceremony comes the much-anticipated “scramble for the offerings,” where locals compete to grab the delicacies. Local beliefs hold that consuming food blessed by the spirits brings good fortune. The ritual also serves as a form of charity, to help villagers who have fallen on hard times.
But the “scramble for the offerings” has become controversial in recent years. As the ritual’s fame has grown — with influencers posting videos of the spectacle on Chinese social media — it has begun to attract large groups of outsiders, who often crowd out those who are truly in need.
Yet, despite its viral popularity, the reality is that today’s Shigu festival is a shadow of its former self. In the early 20th century, practically every household in Chaoshan took part in the festivities and incense burned all month long, according to folk-custom researcher Lin Xuejin.
After 1949, the festivals were suspended for decades, as traditional practices and beliefs were discouraged as “feudal superstitions.” They slowly revived after “reform and opening-up” began in the late 1970s, but mass internal migration and breakneck economic development have also taken their toll.
Today, while villages across Chaoshan still hold Shigu, the monthlong community-wide celebrations have dwindled to one-off collective events on selected days, run almost entirely by older residents. Young people are noticeably scarce in Nansha — except for the gaggle of influencers and creators filming and livestreaming the events.
The Chinese internet’s sudden embrace of Shigu can feel jarring. As Lin chants his appeal to the lonely ghosts before an audience mostly made up of retirees, several drones whir overhead, waiting to capture the excitement of the coming “scramble for the offerings.”
But locals hope the trend can help revive the festival. Several villagers say the influx of content creators has encouraged younger generations to value their local culture more — and pushed older residents to keep organizing the ceremonies despite falling attendance.

articles.title_orig: 5 men arrested near a US-run air base are bailed as UK police probe whether there's a link to Iran
articles.title_zh: 5 men arrested near a US-run air base are bailed as UK police probe whether there's a link to Iran
articles.content_orig:
Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state
Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back.
The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London. They had been arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside early on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.
Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.
An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford.
On Monday, Donald Trump expressed surprise that the suspects had been bailed. The US president said: “I would not have released them.”
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a meeting of the government’s crisis committee Cobra over the events and Iran’s possible role.
An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found.
The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.
He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.
“We have, as you would expect, ensured that our protective security advice and posture remain commensurate to the threat. But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.
Taylor said: “Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain. It can be harder to spot, and to that end I would ask the public to remain vigilant and report anything suspicious to police.”
Trump claimed on Sunday that the men “were looking to do big damage” at the base, used by the US air force, which was taken as revealing a serious terror plot.
Taylor said: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.”
Police said the five men were all from London, one aged 23, three aged 24, and one aged 25. They were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police.
Trump also suggested the plot was known to the US authorities. But British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown.
The base had been at its highest state of alert, called delta, for several days beforehand because of a general threat, with extra security measures.
The farmer said she was surprised it had been left to her to disrupt the activities of the men.
In a round of broadcast interviews, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the woman had only a “partial picture” of the events.
About 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning to a leisure centre, with a 400-metre cordon placed around the white vans as bomb-disposal robots examined them.
At the Labour party conference, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the evacuated residents should shortly be able to return home.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had made threats against RAF Fairford in July.
Iran’s embassy in London denied any involvement in the events in Whelford. It said: “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.
“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”

articles.title_orig: School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play review – comedy makes a near-flawless Broadway debut
articles.title_zh: School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play review – comedy makes a near-flawless Broadway debut
articles.content_orig:
The battle lines are drawn early and definitively in Jocelyn Bioh ‘s School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play . The cruelties come fast and cut deep in this Ghana school lunch room where all the unspoken rules of adolescent pick-or-be-picked-upon are as strict as they are in high schools the world over. Or in other plays and TV shows the world over, whether we’re talking Heathers or Carrie or Jawbreaker . And since Stephen King didn’t write this one, we can be pretty sure there won’t blood, but gruesome playground injuries of a more psychic and soul-crushing variety are entirely on the table.
Bioh, perfectly assisted by her sympatico director Whitney White and a no-weak-link cast, has done something quite amazing with this comedy-drama, opening tonight on Broadway at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre in a first-rate Manhattan Theatre Club production. Bioh takes on the tropes and dramatic conventions of high school claustrophobia, its rebellions and savageries and tendernesses so familiar from ancestors like the franchise that gives this play its subtitle and right up through the newcomer that called John Proctor a villain , that we can only trust a writer of her depth and skills (she wrote Jaja’s African Hair Braiding , after all) to find a new path through the well-trod turf.
And she does. School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play , might well come closest in approach to Kimberly Belflower’s urgent John Proctor Is The Villain in its insistence that homeroom sadism doesn’t just spring from hormones or reindeer game competition. There are larger forces at work, the stuff that hurts people who hurt people, and portraying that hurt (and its goal, escape) with understanding – not to say excuse-making – takes uncommon talent. Belflower showed it, and so does Bioh.
The set up is simple and immediately recognizable. The year is 1986 and the place is a girls boarding school in the Aburi Mountains of Central Ghana. Five of the students – two in their final year, three a year behind – busy themselves with the gossip and whatever else passes for crucial business in the day-to-day, mostly as defined by Paulina ( The Gilded Age ‘s Denée Benton ), the self-anointed queen of the clique by way of her looks, her force of will, her cruel streak and her much admired (if very tenuous) connection to the longed-for America by way of an aunt who lives in New York City and works in a castle there that serves unimaginable culinary delights and who sends Pauline the odd piece of designer clothing that makes her the envy of the school.
We’ll learn that Paulina, far from confident, is so self-conscious of the darkness of her Black skin that she secretly uses toxic bleach products that necessitate frequent trips to the emergency room, that her home life is so impoverished that she unleashes her frustrations on her terrified acolytes. Poor Nana (Erin Morton) gets the worst of the abuse, her large body and constant eating a source of unending bullying from Paulina, who calls her “cow.” Even Paulina’s best friend – a phrase pretty much useless in this milieu – isn’t safe. Ama (Lucia Aremu) pays dearly for the occasional hint of independence, so threatening is free thinking to Paulina.
In the grand tradition of teen movies, the equilibrium of the status quo is disrupted with the arrival of a new student. And Ericka (Jasmine Amy Rogers, all done up in big ’80s hair and a school girl uniform that leaves her unrecognizable from her flapper look in Boop ) is not just any new student. She’s lived in America. She has Bobby Brown’s autograph. She has real Calvin Klein fashions, not the Chinatown knock-offs that have fooled Paulina. And she knows White Castle isn’t a white castle – it isn’t even McDonald’s.
And she has two other things going for her. She’s kind – the put-upon girls of the Aburi Girls Boarding School take to her like docile puppies to a calming stroke – and she’s naturally light-skinned. No harsh chemicals for her, much to the amazement and envy of her Ghanaian classmates. If the mixed-race Ericka doesn’t quite grasp the significance of her coloring – back home at her all-white school she was, to be sure, Black – the other girls certainly do.
And among the things all the girls seem to sense is that Paulina is no longer the shoo-in for the upcoming Miss Ghana try-outs, a realization driven home when the pageant’s recruiter – a former Aburi student who, 20 years previous, won Miss Ghana 1966 and who retains her own mean girl leanings, especially when in the company of the school’s Headmistress, a classmate from those long ago years. One of Bioh’s most telling bits of stage magic here is showing us just how long-lasting such formative role-playing can be. If the device can seem more than a little schematic in intention, its execution – a few lines of dialogue between the recruiter Eloise (Patina Miller) and the Headmistress (Heather Alicia Simms) – nonetheless conveys both the tenacity and bite of mean girldom. And did I mention School Girls is a comedy? And a very funny one at that?
As School Girls builds to its denouement – that pageant try-out – rest assured that Bioh and director White will not deprive us of bearing witness, and the young actors who play the school girls, some in their Broadway debuts, meet the challenge and then some. As they take turns soloing Whitney Houston’s “The Greatest Love of All” – an inspired choice not only for the technical demands that few of these hopefuls could meet, but for Houston’s haunted ending that they couldn’t possible know – the cast members imbue each character with comic ineptitude that’s as poignant as it is laugh-out-loud funny. Even the cruel Paulina’s misplaced overconfidence and comeuppance merits our charity.
Because comeuppance she gets. When the new girl Ericka takes her turn at the solo, her glorious voice rivals that of Whitney herself (as she proved in the otherwise lackluster Boop , Rogers is a talent to watch and embrace). As the greedy recruiter sees something to exploit, and the proud headmistress hears something finally worthy of pride, and the downtrodden classmates have their ding dong the witch is dead moment, poor Paulina all but crumbles into herself (Benton is a marvel in this scene).
But bullies don’t often go away easy. Her face bleeding from the corrosive bleach, her dreams of escape from poverty dashed, Paulina lashes out with ill-gotten information that will take the talented, seemingly charmed Ericka down with her. In the battle that ensues, no one will go untouched by hard truth and the realization of just how stacked the odds against triumph remain in a system where everything from the shade of one’s skin, the geography of one’s home and the capricious nature of one’s parentage determine so much, and foster all sorts of bad behavior and ruthless survivalism.
The Manhattan Theatre Club has given this excellent play the production it deserves. Costume designer Qween Jean, riding high from her Tony-winning contributions to Cats: The Jellicle Ball , delivers the perfect visuals for this tale – the conformity of school uniforms, the explosion of ’80s prom styles for the pageant auditions, the proud African ethnicity of the Headmistress’ attire and the arriviste Americanism of the made-good recruiter – while Teresa L. Williams’ cleverly efficient school cafeteria set, with its large glass windows offering quick hallway peeks at characters in their privacy – gives these school girls ample room for all their towering ambitions and their outsized insecurities.
Not enough praise can be heaped upon the excellent cast (in addition to those mentioned above, there’s the terrific Nia Otchere-Sarfo and Jordan Rice rounding out the clique). Every one of the school girls is perfectly delineated (kudos to the casting team for an exactingly chosen group), with each actor finding the humor, the humanity and, when necessary, the acidity of characters doing their best in a hothouse not of their making. Or not entire

Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway stretches from the Xijin reservoir in Hengzhou, an emerging city in Guangxi, to the Gulf of Tonkin (known as the Beibu Gulf in China), providing southwestern inland provinces with a shorter and more cost-effective route to global markets.
Strategically, it anchors the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a rapidly growing artery that was first conceptualised under the China-Singapore (Chongqing) Connectivity Initiative endorsed in 2015 by President Xi Jinping and Lee Hsien Loong, then prime minister of Singapore.

President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.
The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”
Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023 , but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday , citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.
A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN , showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
A third , which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.
The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.
Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said : “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem , who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)
When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán . “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters .
Rep. Thomas Massie , a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”
Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”
In another Sept. 24 letter , congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “ public service announcements .” A White House official told TIME Thursday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.
A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.
Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act , the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.
In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure .)
“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic warns AI may pose 'existential risks to humanity' in IPO filing: Reuters
articles.title_zh: Anthropic warns AI may pose 'existential risks to humanity' in IPO filing: Reuters
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its IPO that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," an extraordinary warning by a company seeking to profit from the same technology.
The company's IPO prospectus, reviewed by Reuters,  highlights risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit "self-preserving behaviors," including attempts to "resist shutdown," to "conceal or manipulate information" and behavior "resembling blackmail."
"Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm," Anthropic said in the filing.
While public companies routinely outline product risks to investors, few, if any, have issued warnings suggesting their technology could cause potential human extinction. Anthropic emphasized both the transformative potential of AI on par with industrialization and electricity and the irreversible harm it could cause if mishandled.
Anthropic and other AI developers, including OpenAI, have faced scrutiny after incidents where experimental systems defied constraints, including a report of an OpenAI model breaching Australia's health-system database.
Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger estimated a greater than 10% probability that AI could kill humans within the next decade, echoing a sentiment by a former colleague, Jacob Coxon.
The company, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, devoted roughly 80 pages of the 261-page main body of its prospectus to laying out risk factors, nearly twice the 48 pages it used to describe its business.
For comparison, SpaceX, which owns xAI, dedicated just around 38 of the 277-page main body of its prospectus to risk factors.
"Potential model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety," Anthropic said in the prospectus, adding that models sometimes develop unexpected capabilities during training that may not be discovered until they have been deployed and have resulted in significant safety incidents.
AI researchers have also warned that as models grow more capable, they increasingly recognize when they are being watched and adjust their behavior accordingly, which makes it harder to monitor model behavior.
Anthropic declined to comment in response to a request for comment on Monday.
Uncertain returns on safety investment
Despite emphasizing AI safety, Anthropic said that returns on its safety investments are unclear.
It did not disclose in the filing how much the company was spending on such research. Earlier this month, Anthropic said about 6% of the computing power it used for AI research went to safety work in a sample week in July.
The company, creator of Claude AI models, described safety efforts as "resource-intensive" and said it must divide its limited funds between computing power, expensive AI talent and safety.
Anthropic said that its customer usage, and as a result revenue, is driven by new models and that a "continuous and overlapping cadence" of releases is "inherent to remaining at the frontier of AI development."
The company last week released a new version of its Opus model, 10 days after CEO Dario Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for pacing the frontier.
Some analysts and experts have said no leading AI lab would slow down when doing so risks handing rivals an advantage in an industry where valuations can change with each release.
Anthropic has pledged in recent weeks to disclose more data publicly about how it uses AI models to build future generations of the technology, as experts warn about recursive self-improvement — the point at which models can develop on their own without human help.
"We believe building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems is a collective responsibility and that the market will reward it," Anthropic said in the filing.

articles.content_orig:
V is everything to Nothing .
The BTS superstar has joined the tech-forward accessories company as its latest global ambassador, and he debuts by starring in a new campaign modeling Nothing’s new Headphone (1) Pro. Shot in Seoul by Dorothea Sing Zhang, the campaign was fashioned to spotlight the “experimentation and versatility of authentic expression” while reflecting a celebration of technical excellence for both partners.
Described by Nothing as the brand’s “most advanced audio product to date,” the Headphone (1) Pro features a triple-driver architecture comprising a 40-mm bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver and a treble xMEMS driver to deliver detail and immersion across a frequency response range of 20Hz-40kHz. Headphone (1) Pro was tuned with engineers at Metropolis Studios, who helped design a flat equalizer switch to provide a neutral sound profile for producers and creators.
The new offering — created using aluminium paired with titanium for a premium finish with reduced weight — features real-time adaptive active noise cancellation using a 10-mic system to more accurately filter surroundings, especially in audio-challenged settings like windy weather and traffic. The headphones also feature up to 68 hours of battery life.
“I’m excited to be part of this bold new chapter with Nothing,” V said in a statement. “Headphone (1) Pro is a design grounded in creative expression and I look forward to our journey together.”
Added Nothing co-founder and CEO Carl Pei: “V has an instinct for fearless experimentation. He’s always pushing into different sounds and styles; he follows his creative instincts, not tried-and-tested formulas, and that’s exactly what we wanted to capture with Headphone (1) Pro. We’ve built it to give people more freedom and flexibility in everyday listening. V was the perfect choice as we define technical excellence for the next generation of creatives.”
V follows in the footsteps of Charli xcx who joined as a global brand ambassador and investor earlier this year. He’s got big shoes to fill, too, as she helped launch the Headphone (a). As previously reported by The Hollywood Reporter , the $199 headphones sold out across the U.K. and Western Europe within 48 hours following the launch of her campaign directed by her frequent collaborator Aidan Zamiri.
Priced at $399, Headphone (1) Pro hits the market on Sept. 29, 2026, and will be available at nothing.tech, Amazon and nationwide at Best Buy’s North America locations.

articles.title_orig: Nothing’s New Headphone (1) Pro Are Made for the Studio
articles.title_zh: Nothing’s New Headphone (1) Pro Are Made for the Studio
articles.content_orig:
The Headphone (1) Pro is Nothing's newest pair of cans, the company announced on Monday at an evening event in New York City. The headphones resemble Nothing’s first-ever over-ear headphones that debuted last summer , though the design and fit have been refined. The key change, though, is audio quality.
Instead of a single dynamic driver producing the sound in each earcup, Nothing has outfitted the Headphone (1) Pro with three drivers for each ear. Most headphones use a single 40-mm dynamic driver, so a single speaker ends up handling the bass, mids, and treble of your tracks. That can cause some muddiness and distortion. Adding more drivers—one for each specific frequency spectrum—gives the sound more room to stretch out and sparkle.
There’s a 40-mm bass dynamic driver to handle the low end. Then there’s a precision dynamic driver to tackle the midrange sounds like vocals, pianos, and guitars. The company says this driver will render those “S” and “T” sounds with more detail. Finally, there's the treble driver for the highs. Nothing’s driver uses xMEMS technology , which relies on a silicon diaphragm that should make transients—sharp bursts like a cymbal hit or a spiky synth stab—sound clearer.
All of these drivers working together should produce richer sound that’s more detailed overall. Every headphone maker claims their gadget produces the best sound on the market, but at least Nothing has attempted some technical feats here to try to convince you.
What's neat is you can see elements of the triple-driver architecture on the sides of the headphones—Nothing has added a couple of 9H Panda glass panels so you can peep the tech inside. The rest of the headphones are largely aluminum with titanium accents.
You'll no doubt worry about cracking that glass; Nothing claims that it is “shatter- and scratch-resistant," but Philipp Von Lintel, associate principal industrial designer at Nothing, says the glass had to survive durability tests 18 times from a drop of more than 1 meter. Also, the glass construction shouldn't affect repairability much—repair technicians can heat the glass from the outside to remove it and access the internal chamber for fixes. “Even if you crack it, there's a plastic film that keeps the chamber still working,” Von Lintel tells WIRED.
The Headphone (1) Pro is slightly lighter (by 2 grams) than the Headphone (1), with a wider headband and thicker padding, though battery life isn't as long, down to 68 hours with active noise canceling turned off versus 80. It has an IP52 dust- and water-resistance rating , so keep the hood of your rain jacket raised on rainy days.
Almost every gadget maker tosses the “Pro” moniker in the product name to justify a few extra features and a price bump. Yes, the Headphone (1) Pro cost $399, a $100 bump over the standard Headphone (1), but Nothing claims it is specifically catering to not just the average consumer who wants better sound, but also recording artists and audio professionals who work in the studio.
The company is including a feature that activates a flat equalization (EQ) mode—something mix engineers and audio producers prefer when they’re working—that’s triggered by a physical button on the headphones. Nothing collaborated with Metropolis Studio , a pro recording studio, to make the EQ features. There's even a “Studio B” Dynamic Spatial Audio mode that simulates Metropolis' mixing room, and four other Custom EQ profiles, like Concert Hall or Club. And yes, there’s a 3.5-mm jack so you can plug in (or stick with hi-res wireless or USB-C).
Charlie Smith, Nothing’s chief brand officer, says people will want these headphones for their commute to work. “That's fine, but people are making music on the go and need studio-level sound wherever they are," he says.
Nothing also claims the headphones have the best active noise cancellation it’s ever shipped, thanks to the use of 10 microphones to filter out ambient sounds. (Apple's AirPods Max , for comparison, use eight.)
“To us, this is a flagship product where we're able to showcase what we can do," Smith says. “It also helps elevate us as a brand.”
Sadly, they don’t fold up. Instead, Nothing is following Apple’s lead by including a bra-like carry case to keep the cans protected.
They'll officially hit store shelves on September 29—not only on Nothing's online store and Amazon, but also nationwide in Best Buy stores across North America.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices rise on continued Middle East supply concerns
articles.title_zh: Oil prices rise on continued Middle East supply concerns
articles.content_orig:
If you think your energy costs are high now, the situation may be about to get a whole lot worse.
With traffic in the Strait of Hormuz – normally the primary route for oil leaving the Middle East – hovering below 15% of prewar levels , oil prices have increased from US$65 a barrel before the conflict in Iran began in February 2026 to more than $100 a barrel in mid-September.
When the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran, analysts feared prices would soon reach $150 or even $200 a barrel. That hasn’t happened yet. But seven months into the conflict, with no clear end in sight, the global oil market has now largely exhausted the safety measures that exist to keep a lid on petroleum prices.
As researchers who study the relationship between energy and national security , we have been following these dynamics throughout the conflict, and the oil market is now showing signs that significant price hikes – and perhaps even shortages – may be on the way.
Some oil has been able to make it out of the Persian Gulf despite the closure of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia increased output via its East-West pipeline , which runs from Abqaiq on the Persian Gulf overland to Yanbu on the coast of the Red Sea. At full capacity, that pipeline can carry as much as 7 million barrels per day , although only about 4 million to 5 million barrels per day are typically exported.
But attacks on the pipeline in mid-September that Saudi Arabia blames on Iran-backed militias based in Iraq forced the Saudis to temporarily halt oil shipments through that pipeline. The pipeline has now restarted operations at very low volumes, but it will likely take at least six to eight weeks to regain full capacity. Even this short cessation has tightened already constrained oil markets, and the threat of further Houthi attacks on Red Sea oil exports will only add to inflationary pressures.
Meanwhile, in Russia, Ukrainian drone attacks have damaged refineries , reducing Russian production of diesel fuel and prompting the country to ban exports of it . That has removed another 3% of the global daily supply of diesel, an important fuel for trucking and shipping . When diesel costs go up, the result is inflation in the cost of goods across the global economy.
In the U.S., 47 states experienced record-high diesel prices on Sept. 22, with the national average reaching $6.52 per gallon.
The high prices prompted President Donald Trump to threaten to ban diesel exports , a move analysts suggest would make matters worse by accentuating global supply shortages and driving world prices upward .
Beyond diesel, motor oil prices have quadrupled , and supply shortages are starting to take hold. For instance, Costco has almost doubled its prices for motor oil and has limited the amount customers can buy.
The upshot from all this is that Americans are spending a lot more on fuel in 2026 as compared to 2025. Between March 1 and late September, Americans spent an additional $72 billion on gasoline compared to the same period a year ago, as well as $45 billion more on diesel.  That’s $117 billion in additional fuel costs, above and beyond the costs of the war itself, which the Pentagon estimated at $45 billion as of early September.
These shocks are even more acute outside the United States, which is the world’s largest energy producer. South and Southeast Asian countries, which were more reliant on imports from the Persian Gulf than the United States, were hit hard soon after the war broke out. Some of them have had to ration fuel , while others enacted emergency measures like shortening the work or school week to reduce fuel use .
These challenges are now hitting Europe hard as well. On Sept. 20, some 15% of French service stations had reportedly run out of either diesel or gas .
The international community has already taken most of the measures available to curb oil demand and boost its supply. Those moves have reduced the scale of oil price increases, but they did not prevent them entirely. Now, the toolbox is largely empty, leaving prices on the brink of spiking again.
In March 2026, a coordinated effort among 32 countries released more than 400 million barrels of oil into the global market from those countries’ strategic reserves. Those stockpiles are now substantially depleted, and it is not clear how much additional oil that countries will be willing or even able to release as the war continues.
Since the war began, the United States alone has released 130 million barrels , leaving its reserves at a 40-year low . The U.S. may not be able to release much more without compromising the structural integrity of the salt caverns where the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is stored.
China has played the largest role in containing global oil prices to date by releasing official reserves as well as what now seem to be massive additional reserves not previously disclosed to the public . The country reduced its crude oil imports by nearly 50% between February and June 2026.
The increased electrification of the Chinese economy played a key role in reducing Chinese demand for oil during this period. More than 60% of new passenger car sales in China are electric vehicles or plug-in hybrids, and 30% of its heavy truck sales are now electric.
Overall, China’s electrification of its transport sector allowed it to reduce oil consumption by 1.35 million barrels per day in the first half of 2026.
Other countries are looking to China for help as well. The country’s international sales of electric vehicles, batteries and solar panels have skyrocketed , as other countries seek to insulate themselves from oil market shocks.
Less encouragingly when it comes to greenhouse gas emissions, China has used more coal to offset oil demand and as an alternative means of petrochemical production as well.
Of perhaps more immediate concern, China’s oil demand is now starting to creep up again, with crude imports rising 6.2% in August 2026 as compared with the previous month. Even if its imports don’t reach prewar levels any time soon, increased Chinese demand, coupled with a tighter oil market, may result in additional price hikes over the next few weeks.
China still has about four to six months of stockpiles, including commercial and strategic reserves, but Beijing may soon seek to gradually restock its inventories , although the Chinese may postpone these purchases if prices continue to soar.
Sustained conflict in Iran – itself a major oil producer – continued disruptions of oil shipments in the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran-linked militias’ disruptions to shipping in the Red Sea could mean the reemergence of the nightmare scenarios analysts envisioned when the fighting began.
It’s not clear if that would translate into simply much higher prices at the pump or turn into 1970s-style shortages , where there’s not enough fuel available at any price and lines stretch around the block at gas stations.
With the 2026 midterm elections looming, the White House will want to avoid that scenario at all costs. But the Trump administration has already released large amounts from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and has rejected policies that would have reduced oil demand, such as stricter fuel economy standards or incentives for electric vehicle adoption.
At this point, Trump has relatively few options available to blunt new price shocks, the effects of which may be visible not just at the pump but also at the ballot box.

Raoni Barcelos was rushed to a hospital after losing to Raul Rosas Jr.
Raoni Barcelos released a video from his hospital bed almost 48 hours after his scary defeat to Raul Rosas Jr. to confirm he’s “doing well” and already anticipates a “stronger” return.
Barcelos had his five-fight winning streak snapped in the main event of UFC Vegas 121, which went down this past Saturday at the Meta APEX in Las Vegas, after collapsing unconscious in the fifth round in his bantamweight clash. The 39-year-old veteran shared a short statement Monday morning to say he was “doing great,” and thank fans on a video post hours later.
“Hey everyone, how’s it going?” Barcelos said in Portuguese. “I’m here to send you a message and let you know that I’m doing well. I’m doing really well and undergoing all the exams here at the hospital. This is just the hospital’s protocol, so I have to go through all of them. That’s it, guys. I want to thank everyone for all the prayers and all the kind messages. Please keep sending that positive energy.”
Barcelos was ahead in the scorecards and likely three minutes away from a decision win — had they gone the distance — before passing out in the clinch and needing immediate medical assistance, getting transported to a local hospital. Rosas Jr. was declared the winner by technical knockout.
“We move forward, on to the next one,” Barcelos said. “I gave everything I had inside that cage. Like I said before, I was only leaving that cage if I was carried out, and that’s exactly how it happened. It wasn’t the way I wanted it to be. I wanted to become champion and leave with the victory, but God knows everything. So we move on to the next one.
“I’m here, doing well. I’ll be back, and I’ll come back stronger. And I want to send all of you a kiss and a big hug. Thank you so much for everything. Thank you, and let’s keep moving forward!”

HOUSTON -- The Astros will turn to rookie right-hander AJ Blubaugh to start Tuesday’s Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series against the White Sox at Daikin Park. Blubaugh -- who threw 15 pitches in relief Friday against the A’s, allowing one run in two-thirds of an inning -- will serve as an opener.
Astros ace right-hander Hunter Brown will start Game 2 on Wednesday on normal rest, a source told MLB.com. Houston would then have right-hander Hayden Wesneski lined up for a possible Game 3 on Thursday.
Blubaugh led the Major Leagues with 27 relief appearances of at least two innings this season, the most by an Astros pitcher since Dave Veres had 27 in 1995. He led all relievers with a career-high 96 innings. Blubaugh has thrown more than two innings in only five games this year.
The most recent Astros rookie to start a postseason game was Luis Garcia in Game 6 of the 2021 World Series, but the Astros have never started a rookie in Game 1 of a postseason series.
Blubaugh faced the White Sox three times this season, allowing no runs, four hits and two walks while striking out three in four innings.
The Astros used six pitchers to cover nine innings in Sunday’s 9-0 win over the A’s in West Sacramento, a game Houston needed to win to return to the playoffs. Peter Lambert, pitching on two days of rest, threw 41 pitches in two innings and won’t be an option for bulk innings Tuesday. Neither will rookie starter Ethan Pecko, who threw 34 pitches in three scoreless innings Sunday.
Beyond that, the Astros’ bullpen is rested. Miguel Ullola threw 18 pitches Sunday, Bryan Abreu hasn’t pitched since Thursday and closer Josh Hader hasn’t pitched since Wednesday. All would be options to cover some innings in Game 1.

articles.title_orig: The Trump administration weakens fuel efficiency standards for new cars
articles.title_zh: The Trump administration weakens fuel efficiency standards for new cars
articles.content_orig:
Traffic moves along the 405 Freeway on Feb. 13 in Los Angeles. Apu Gomes/Getty Images hide caption
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help
The Trump administration announced Monday it's scaling back how fuel efficient American carmakers need to make their fleets.
The Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards set average fuel economy levels for carmakers. The revised rules, which were finalized Monday, will now require carmakers to make their new passenger car and truck fleets up to 1% more fuel efficient each year, aiming for an average of 34.9 miles to the gallon in model year 2031.
This is down from Biden-era rules, which required an annual 2% increase in fuel efficiency with a goal of most vehicles getting, on average, 50.4 miles to the gallon by 2031.
The rationale: affordability. Administration officials argue that fuel efficiency technology is expensive, and has helped to drive up the cost of vehicles. They estimate that scaling back the standards will shave about $1,300 off the sticker prices of new cars.
"This administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in an online statement announcing the change.
President Trump weighed in over the weekend on Truth Social : "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car."
Climate advocates and auto industry observers say the rules change is another step in the Trump administration's efforts to roll back Biden-era climate policies — including cutting the federal tax credit for electric vehicle buyers , delaying federal dollars for a nationwide EV charging program , and striking down federal waivers that let California set its own strict pollution regulations.
In a statement emailed to NPR, Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the Center for Biological Diversity, wrote that rolling back the standards would increase gasoline usage and pollution, "costing consumers at the pump and at the doctor's office."
"Trump is tanking sensible mileage standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who're getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump," he continued.
According to AAA , the national average price for gasoline today is close to $4.50 a gallon, and for diesel, a gallon is hovering close to $6.50, just short of last week's record high.
Easing CAFE standards will hinder the industry's realignment toward more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles, said economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University. "It's very bad in the long term, because it slows progress," she said. "Then we make our auto companies less competitive. We give them less practice in making the cars that both Americans will want in the future and that the rest of the world will want." After all, American carmakers hope to continue selling their cars in foreign markets that may have stricter emissions standards. And a future presidential administration could change the rules again.
CAFE standards have been part of the auto industry for decades. In 1975, during that decade's great oil supply shock, Congress enacted rules that encouraged carmakers to make their fleets more fuel efficient in an effort to reduce Americans' dependency on the Middle East for oil.
Since then, the national conversation about fuel efficiency has changed; the U.S. is now the world's largest oil producer, and many regulatory changes have instead been driven by concerns about climate change. Since the early 2010s, the fuel efficiency requirements for passenger cars and light trucks have consistently risen .
In practice, the Biden-era standards meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles to balance out their gas guzzlers — otherwise they were subject to a fine.
But the Trump administration dropped that penalty last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effectively defanging the Biden-era CAFE standards. In December, the White House proposed scaling them back altogether. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened a period of public comment .
In its final rule announcing the change, NHTSA also said it's eliminating the ability of carmakers to trade credits amongst themselves for making electric vehicles — a part of the Biden-era CAFE Standards that Republicans often criticized. This rule allowed automakers to buy credits from EV manufacturers to offset making less fuel-efficient vehicles. This helped them meet their CAFE targets.
In announcing the new change, the administration said lowering the CAFE standards will make cars cheaper.
"Instead of allowing manufacturers to design and produce vehicles they believe their customers will want and need, while spreading real-world fuel economy improvements across their fleets, the system has increasingly led manufacturers to try to fit square vehicle pegs in round classification holes to force the adoption of technologies that do not meet the demands of American families," stated NHTSA in the final rule. "All of this adds inefficiency and cost — pushing even more consumers out of an already unaffordable new car market."
"It's true that the price of new cars has gone up quite a lot," says Helper at Case Western. But she contends that much of that is not because of fuel economy standards. Instead, she says, it's because vehicles have gotten larger, they've faced tariffs and supply chain issues in recent years, and they are often loaded with extras like infotainment systems.
A Consumer Reports analysis from 2023 found that between model years 2003 and 2021, vehicles got about 30% more fuel efficient, but attributed the rise in prices to an industrywide shift toward expensive SUVs, rather than from using more fuel-efficient technologies.
And when it comes to the monthly costs of a new car, there are external factors beyond a carmaker's control — like the cost of an auto loan , which is affected both by the Federal Reserve's benchmark lending rate and by an individual buyer's credit score.
"One of the cruxes of vehicle affordability right now is the average monthly payment getting jacked up, because interest rates are so high," says Ellen Hughes-Cromwick, who spent much of her career as Ford's chief global economist and now studies clean energy as a senior visiting fellow at the center-left Third Way think tank.
Plus, a cut in the sticker price might eventually be offset by spending on gas. If vehicles are less fuel efficient, that means drivers will need to fill up at the pump more often — which is especially salient in a year of high gas prices due to the war in Iran.
For now, American carmakers are stuck in a kind of jam.
On the one hand, Helper said, a rules change that makes it easier for them to sell trucks and SUVs is "good in the short-term, because they make a lot of profits making these giant vehicles," though they are not as popular outside of the U.S.
This new move "allows the U.S. more of a playground in this protected little Galapagos of an ecosystem where no one else is wanting to compete," Helper continued.
But the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group representing car and light-truck manufacturers that sell vehicles to the U.S. and that includes automakers such as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, praised the move. "We're still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions," said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the alliance, in an emailed statement to NPR.
"The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand. Today's final rule is an appropriate course correction," he continued.
